welcome_dialog.title: Welcome to CARA
welcome_dialog.message:
Thanks for installing CARA.

As this is your first time starting the application, I would recommend that you take a quick look at the Getting Started section of the manual.

It covers the most important aspects of configuring and using CARA, so that you will hopefully have a great time and enjoy using the application.

You will also find a link to CARA's YouTube channel with many tutorial videos
in the Help menu.

If you enjoy the project, please consider leaving a Star on the GitHub repository, subscribing to and liking the YouTube channel/videos, and spreading the word!

Best regards, Philipp.

custom_endpoint_disclaimer.title: Custom Endpoint Disclaimer
custom_endpoint_disclaimer.message:
Experimental feature: Custom endpoint support is an experimental implementation. Responses from locally run models may not match the quality of top-tier cloud models (e.g. OpenAI GPT-4, Anthropic Claude).

Local models may be less accurate, less consistent, or occasionally produce incorrect or irrelevant answers. Use at your own discretion.

messages.incomplete_analysis:
Bulk Analysis has been aborted due to a failed integrity check (incomplete analysis results).

The integrity check failed on {game_label}.

This can happen, if the operating system went into stand-by mode or similar circumstances leading to the UCI engine not providing complete results. Games which successfully completed remain analyzed, so you can resume bulk analysis by running it again and leaving the Re-analyze already analyzed games checkmark unchecked.
messages.standby_warning: It is advisable to deactivate standby and power-saving mode in the host operating system during analysis. This is especially relevant if the computer is not plugged in and is running on battery.

copy.welcome_body:
Stockfish is a free, open-source chess engine and the easiest way to get started with analysis in CARA.

This assistant will download an official Stockfish build for your computer, save it to a folder you choose, and add it to CARA.

shallow.help_text:
Check Logs — what the chips mean

Check Logs reads each answer on its own.

Shallow (3x3) marks a Why answer that could fit almost any move: it doesn't name a piece, square, plan, threat or idea from this position. Short answers are fine if they're concrete. Answers that repeat each other from a different angle are fine too.

Shallow (CLAMP / CCT) marks a note that gives no diagnosis of the move: it only says you don't understand why the move was bad, it isn't about the move at all, or it writes the move off without saying what you missed, intended, or should have played. Any concrete point — a hung piece, a missed tactic, your intent, a better move — makes it Deep. CLAMP and CCT notes have no lesson, so they never get a Vague chip.

Vague marks a lesson that gives you nothing to do next game. A concrete habit or check counts as a real lesson, even a short one, such as "count attackers and defenders". Shrugs and "try harder" are vague.

Blank answers are never flagged.

Ignore stops a chip from coming back. To undo it, untick Ignore in Show Logged Moments and click Save. If you edit an answer, its Ignore is cleared and the answer is checked again.

Every run checks every answer again from its current text. Nothing is saved into your games until you click Save.

shallow.tooltip_3x3: This answer could fit almost any move. Name a piece, square, plan or threat from this position. Tick Ignore if you disagree.
shallow.tooltip_clamp_cct: This note doesn't diagnose the move. Say what you missed, what you intended, or what you should have played. Tick Ignore if you disagree.

vague_lesson.tooltip: This lesson gives you nothing to do next game. Name a concrete habit or check, such as "count attackers and defenders". Tick Ignore if you disagree.

regex_editor.title: Edit regular expression

examples.label: Several spellings of a name
examples.tooltip: Matches any of these spellings. Use on White or Black. Search ignores case. Edit the highlighted names.

examples.label: Any of these players
examples.tooltip: Matches any of these last names. Use on White or Black. For either color, add the same pattern on both rows and join them with OR. Edit the highlighted names.

examples.label: A last name
examples.tooltip: Matches every player with this last name, such as Carlsen, Magnus. Use on the player selection, or on White or Black. Edit the highlighted name.

examples.label: A first name
examples.tooltip: Matches a given name after the comma, such as Morphy, Paul. Pauline is left out. Use on the player selection, or on White or Black. Edit the highlighted name.

examples.label: Last name starts with
examples.tooltip: Matches last names that start with this letter, such as Murphy, Paul. Use on the player selection, or on White or Black. Edit the highlighted letter.

examples.label: Last name with van, von, or de
examples.tooltip: Matches a particle before the last name, such as van Foreest, Jorden. Use on the player selection, or on White or Black. Edit the highlighted words.

examples.label: Player titles (GM/IM/FM/…)
examples.tooltip: Matches common title prefixes such as GM, IM, FM, WGM, and NM, including an optional period. Use on White or Black. Edit the highlighted title list to add more.

examples.label: Rating in parentheses
examples.tooltip: Matches a 3–4 digit rating inside parentheses, as in a player name. Example: "Carlsen (2830)".

examples.label: Non-digits
examples.tooltip: Matches everything that is not a digit. Useful when cleaning WhiteElo / BlackElo values such as "elo 2755".

examples.label: Online site
examples.tooltip: Matches a common online site. Use on Site. Edit the highlighted list.

examples.label: Round number
examples.tooltip: Matches "Round" followed by a number. Use on Event.

examples.label: Trailing federation code
examples.tooltip: Matches a trailing 3-letter federation code, optionally in [ ] or ( ). Use on Site or Event. Example: "Wijk aan Zee NED" or "Berlin [GER]".

examples.label: Time-control fragment
examples.tooltip: Matches time-control tokens such as 10+0, 15+10, G/90, or 15|10 inside an event name. Use on Event.

examples.label: First 4-digit year
examples.tooltip: Captures the first four-digit year in an event name. Example: "London 2024 Open" → "2024".

examples.label: First three words
examples.sample: Tata Steel Masters Wijk aan Zee
examples.tooltip: Captures the first three whitespace-separated words of an event or site name.

examples.label: Keep text before "-"
examples.tooltip: Matches an event name and captures the text before the dash. Example: "Wijk aan Zee - Masters".

examples.label: Keep text after "-"
examples.tooltip: Captures the text after the dash. Example: "Wijk aan Zee - Masters" → "Masters".

examples.label: Keep text before ","
examples.tooltip: Captures the text before the first comma. Example: "Candidates, Toronto".

examples.label: Keep text after ","
examples.tooltip: Captures the text after the last comma. Example: "Candidates, Toronto" → "Toronto".

examples.label: Keep text inside (…)
examples.tooltip: Captures the text inside the first pair of parentheses. Example: "Olympiad (Open)" → "Open".

examples.label: Keep text before (…)
examples.tooltip: Captures the text before the first parenthesis. Example: "Olympiad (Open)" → "Olympiad".

examples.label: Games from one year
examples.tooltip: Matches dates in 2024, such as 2024.03.18. Use on Date. Edit the highlighted year.

examples.label: A span of years
examples.tooltip: Matches dates from 2015 through 2024. Use on Date. Edit the highlighted numbers for another span.

examples.label: One month
examples.tooltip: Matches November in a PGN date (YYYY.MM.DD). Use on Date. Edit the highlighted month.

examples.label: Unknown month or day
examples.tooltip: Matches ??, which PGN uses for an unknown month or day. Use on Date. Example: 1999.??.??.

examples.label: ECO letter group
examples.tooltip: Matches every ECO code in group B, such as B22. Use on ECO. Edit the highlighted letter (A–E).

examples.label: Opening names
examples.tooltip: Matches any of these opening names. Use on Event, or on a custom tag such as Opening. Edit the highlighted names.

examples.label: Clock with an increment
examples.tooltip: Matches a clock with an increment, such as 300+5 or 180+2. Use on TimeControl. The pattern sees the original tag, not the base seconds.

examples.label: Seconds and no increment
examples.tooltip: Matches a clock that is only a number of seconds, such as 300 for five minutes and no increment. Use on TimeControl.

examples.label: Moves and time
examples.tooltip: Matches a classical control written as moves/seconds, such as 40/7200. Use on TimeControl.

examples.label: Correspondence clock (- or *)
examples.tooltip: Matches a missing clock written as - or *. Use on TimeControl.

examples.label: Bullet or blitz
examples.tooltip: Matches the Bullet or Blitz category. Use on TC Type, which stores the category name rather than the clock. Edit the highlighted names (Rapid and Classical work the same way).

explain.capturing_group: Capturing group #{number}. Groups multiple tokens together and creates a capture group for extracting a substring or using a backreference.
explain.noncapturing_group: Non-capturing group. Groups tokens without creating a backreference.
explain.positive_lookahead: Positive lookahead. Matches the enclosed pattern ahead, without consuming it.
explain.negative_lookahead: Negative lookahead. Succeeds when the enclosed pattern does not match ahead.
explain.positive_lookbehind: Positive lookbehind. Matches the enclosed pattern behind, without consuming it.
explain.negative_lookbehind: Negative lookbehind. Succeeds when the enclosed pattern does not match behind.
explain.named_group: Named group "{name}" (#{number}). A capture group you can refer to by name.
explain.backreference: Backreference. Matches the same text as capturing group #{number}.
explain.named_backreference: Backreference. Matches the same text as the group named "{name}".
explain.flags: Flags ({flags}). Changes matching options from here on.
explain.flags_group: Flags group ({flags}). Applies those options inside the group only.
explain.character_set: Character set. Match any character in the set.
explain.negated_set: Negated set. Match any character that is not in the set.
explain.range: Range. Matches a character in the range "{start}" to "{end}" (char code {start_code} to {end_code}).{case_note}
explain.not_digit: Not a digit. Matches any character that is not a digit.
explain.word: Word. Matches any word character (alphanumeric and underscore).
explain.not_word: Not a word character. Matches any character that is not a letter, digit, or underscore.
explain.whitespace: Whitespace. Matches a space, tab, or line break.
explain.not_whitespace: Not whitespace. Matches any character that is not whitespace.
explain.word_boundary: Word boundary. Matches the edge between a word character and something else.
explain.not_word_boundary: Not a word boundary. Matches a position that is not the edge of a word.
explain.start_string: Start of the text. Matches only at the beginning.
explain.end_string: End of the text. Matches only at the end.
explain.any: Any character. Matches any character except a newline.
explain.start_anchor: Start. Matches the beginning of the text.
explain.end_anchor: End. Matches the end of the text.
explain.alternation: Alternation. Match either the expression before or the expression after.
explain.quantifier_zero_or_more: Quantifier. Match 0 or more of the preceding token.{lazy_note}
explain.quantifier_one_or_more: Quantifier. Match 1 or more of the preceding token.{lazy_note}
explain.quantifier_zero_or_one: Quantifier. The preceding token is optional.{lazy_note}
explain.quantifier_exact: Quantifier. Match the preceding token exactly {n} times.{lazy_note}
explain.quantifier_at_least: Quantifier. Match the preceding token at least {n} times.{lazy_note}
explain.quantifier_at_most: Quantifier. Match the preceding token at most {m} times.{lazy_note}
explain.quantifier_between: Quantifier. Match the preceding token between {n} and {m} times.{lazy_note}

_examples.weight_by_phase_distribution: max(5.0, min(100.0, 100.0 - ((average_cpl_opening * opening_moves + average_cpl_middlegame * middlegame_moves + average_cpl_endgame * endgame_moves) / max(total_moves, 1) / 3.5)))
_examples.bonus_for_consistent_phases: max(5.0, min(100.0, 100.0 - (average_cpl / 3.5) + (10.0 - abs(average_cpl_opening - average_cpl) - abs(average_cpl_middlegame - average_cpl) - abs(average_cpl_endgame - average_cpl)) * 0.5))

elo_estimation.formula: (max(0, int(2800 - (average_cpl * 8.5) - ((blunder_rate * 50 + mistake_rate * 20) * 40) - max(0, (average_cpl_opening - average_cpl) * 5)))) / 1.995 + 233 if max(0, int(2800 - (average_cpl * 8.5) - ((blunder_rate * 50 + mistake_rate * 20) * 40) - max(0, (average_cpl_opening - average_cpl) * 5))) < 2172 else (max(0, int(2800 - (average_cpl * 8.5) - ((blunder_rate * 50 + mistake_rate * 20) * 40) - max(0, (average_cpl_opening - average_cpl) * 5)))) / 0.33 - 5261

_examples.normalized_default: max(0, int(2800 - (average_cpl * 8.5) - ((blunder_rate * 50 + mistake_rate * 20) * 40))) / 1.918 + 166 if max(0, int(2800 - (average_cpl * 8.5) - ((blunder_rate * 50 + mistake_rate * 20) * 40))) < 2207 else (max(0, int(2800 - (average_cpl * 8.5) - ((blunder_rate * 50 + mistake_rate * 20) * 40)))) / 0.311 - 5780
_examples.normalized_simple: max(0, int(2800 - (average_cpl * 10))) / 1.681 - 39 if max(0, int(2800 - (average_cpl * 10))) < 2271 else max(0, int(2800 - (average_cpl * 10))) / 0.268 - 7162
_examples.normalized_accuracy_based: max(0, int(accuracy * 28)) / 1.349 - 450 if max(0, int(accuracy * 28)) < 2376 else max(0, int(accuracy * 28)) / 0.214 - 9790
_examples.normalized_penalize_weak_opening: max(0, int(2800 - (average_cpl * 8.5) - ((blunder_rate * 50 + mistake_rate * 20) * 40) - max(0, (average_cpl_opening - average_cpl) * 5))) / 1.995 + 233 if max(0, int(2800 - (average_cpl * 8.5) - ((blunder_rate * 50 + mistake_rate * 20) * 40) - max(0, (average_cpl_opening - average_cpl) * 5))) < 2172 else max(0, int(2800 - (average_cpl * 8.5) - ((blunder_rate * 50 + mistake_rate * 20) * 40) - max(0, (average_cpl_opening - average_cpl) * 5))) / 0.33 - 5261
_examples.consider_phase_balance: max(0, int(2800 - (average_cpl * 8.5) - ((blunder_rate * 50 + mistake_rate * 20) * 40) - (abs(average_cpl_opening - average_cpl_middlegame) + abs(average_cpl_middlegame - average_cpl_endgame)) * 2))

chess_log.narrative_system:
You are a chess coach helping a player reflect on their self-annotated game moments. Be specific, encouraging, and concrete. Avoid generic advice. Write in second person ('you', 'your'). If a category's counts across bins don't show a consistent direction, say so plainly rather than forcing a trend narrative — but still report any genuine qualitative insight from that category's why-notes even when the numeric trend is inconclusive. A small or irregular count doesn't mean there's nothing worth learning from what you actually wrote. Write in plain, direct sentences. Never use em-dashes anywhere in your response, for any purpose - including setting off lists of numbers or parenthetical asides. Use commas, periods, or separate sentences instead. Don't lose the underlying connections between categories when the data supports them (e.g. if a hung piece and a dangerous alignment happen on the same tagged moment, say so directly, just without the flourish). Refer to time periods using their actual calendar labels (e.g. specific months or date ranges) provided in the data. Never use generic placeholder language like 'periods' or 'bins' when a real time label is available. Structure your response as three markdown sections, in this exact order, using exactly these headers:

## Patterns & Recurrent Themes
## Tactical Breakdown
## Key Takeaways

The Patterns & Recurrent Themes section is a markdown bullet list — emit it as 2 to 4 bullet items (one per theme) using `-` as the bullet marker, with a blank line separating each bullet's body from the next bullet. Each bullet must begin with a bold sentence-fragment lead-in that names the theme in 3 to 8 words, followed by a period, then 2 to 5 sentences of body text (e.g. `- **Rushing calculation in sharp positions.** You repeatedly ...`). The lead-in must stand on its own as a scannable summary of the theme. Do NOT nest bullets; do NOT emit sub-bullets. Focus on the underlying behavioral tendencies (rushing calculation, drifting attention in slow positions, missing prophylaxis, etc.), keep the tone player-focused, and do NOT frame around CLAMP letters or percentages — category-level detail belongs in the Tactical Breakdown section that follows. The Tactical Breakdown section MUST be a markdown pipe table with exactly three columns and a header row, in this exact format:

| Skill | Observed Issue | Strategic Impact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ... | ... | ... |

One row per chess-concept theme that the data supports. In the Skill column, use generic chess-concept labels that you synthesize from the underlying moves and why-notes — for example: King Safety, Piece Coordination, Pawn Structure, Calculation Depth, Time Management, Move Order, Tactical Awareness, Prophylaxis. Do NOT use CLAMP letters, CLAMP category names (Checks, Loose Pieces and Squares, Alignments, Mobility Restrictions, Passed Pawns), CCT category names (Checks, Captures, Threats), or 3x3 Why-question labels in the Skill column — treat those as grouping hints only and name the underlying chess concept instead. This is where per-concept percentages and pattern-level observations belong — not in Patterns & Recurrent Themes. Do not repeat the same content across multiple rows. Do not add extra columns. Every row MUST populate all three columns with substantive content — never emit a row where Strategic Impact is empty, whitespace, a placeholder like — or N/A, or a restatement of the Observed Issue. Strategic Impact must name the concrete downstream consequence for the game (material loss, king exposure, initiative surrendered, tempo wasted, etc.). If you cannot articulate a distinct Strategic Impact for a row, drop the row entirely rather than emit a blank cell. Do not emit any prose outside the table in this section. The Key Takeaways section is the single most important part of your response and must never be dropped or reduced to a throwaway line. Write it as 1 to 3 short paragraphs of continuous prose, not a numbered or bulleted list. Each paragraph must begin with a bold sentence-fragment lead-in that names the actionable takeaway in 3 to 8 words, followed by a period, then the paragraph body (e.g. `**Slow down in king-attack positions.** When the tagged notes mention...`). Each paragraph must be anchored to a specific quote or short phrase drawn verbatim from the player's own why-notes or whole-game notes, and use that anchor to name a concrete, actionable next step. Do not restate the earlier sections in miniature and do not offer generic coaching advice that isn't tied to the player's own words. If you are running short on space, compress or omit low-signal rows in the Tactical Breakdown table (few tagged moments, no clear trend, such as Mobility or Passed Pawns when sparse) rather than sacrifice anything in Key Takeaways. When discussing a category's trend across periods, do not mechanically list every period's name and number in a row more than once. Refer to the overall pattern in plain language (e.g. 'consistently across all four logged periods,' 'in every period without exception') and name specific periods only when calling out a genuine standout (the highest or lowest, or a real change point), not as a rote enumeration. When a preset's category letters are not all distinct (as with CCT, where both Checks and Captures start with C), never use a bare letter as shorthand for either one. Always use the full category name (Checks, Captures, Threats) to keep them unambiguous. This does not apply to CLAMP, where each letter maps to exactly one category and bare-letter shorthand (C, L, A, M, P) remains fine. For CCT-tagged moments, a tag can describe either side of the board. A Checks, Captures, or Threats tag may mean the player's own candidate move created that problem, or it may mean the opponent's prior move created it and the player failed to respond to it. Read the why-note itself to tell which; do not assume a tag always means 'the player's move was the problem.' When you cite a specific move from a game, always give the full move+color pairing: 'move number. move, White vs Black' (for example, '16. b4, NotThePainter vs mattsartin'). Never abbreviate to just 'vs Black' or 'the b4 move' — the reader needs the move number, the SAN, and the player-color pairing every time. Cap verbatim quotes from the player's why-notes at 1 to 2 per theme, per table row, and per Key Takeaway paragraph. Do not sprinkle a quote into every sentence — pick the one or two that best carry the point and let them do the work.

narrative_glossaries.CLAMP:
- C — Checks: A checking move — either one the opponent's last move enabled that wasn't accounted for, or one the player's own candidate move allows in return.
- L — Loose Pieces and Squares: A piece or square left undefended or under-defended — the opponent's loose piece going unclaimed, or one of the player's own left hanging by their candidate move.
- A — Alignments: A dangerous lineup along a file, rank, diagonal, or knight's reach — enabling pins, skewers, forks, or discovered attacks — whether the opponent's last move created it unnoticed, or the player's own candidate move creates it against themselves.
- M — Mobility Restrictions: A piece left with restricted movement and at risk of being trapped — an opponent's piece that could have been cornered, or one of the player's own boxed in by their candidate move.
- P — Passed Pawns: A pawn positioned to become unstoppable — the opponent's passed pawn not dealt with in time, or the player's own candidate move handing them one.
narrative_glossaries.CCT:
- C — Checks: A checking move — either one the opponent's last move enabled that wasn't accounted for, or one the player's own candidate move allows in return.
- C — Captures: A piece or square left undefended or under-defended, the opponent's loose piece going unclaimed, or one of the player's own left hanging by their candidate move.
- T — Threats: An aggressive move, such as attacking a higher-value piece, creating a mating sequence, or setting up a tactical fork, that forces the opponent to respond defensively on their very next turn to avoid immediate material or positional loss.

chess_log.narrative_3x3_structure:
## Why-note structure — 3x3

Each 3x3-tagged moment may include answers to up to four questions, always asked in this order, though the player may skip any of them:

1. Why did I choose that move?
2. Why is my move not ideal?
3. Why is the better move better than my chosen move?
4. What do I do in the future so this doesn't happen again?

These are the four questions from GM Noel Studer's 3x3 method. Together, the four answers form one connected reasoning chain about a single decision: Why1 establishes the player's intent, Why2 identifies what was wrong with their chosen move, Why3 explains why the better move is better -- this is often the same underlying point as Why2 restated from a different angle, not always a distinct second step, so don't force them into a strict cause-then-effect sequence if the player's own answers don't split that way -- and Why4 names the lesson for next time. Either Why2 or Why3, or both, may be blank. Treat a blank as simply unanswered, not as a break in the chain. All four always describe the player's own chosen move and their own reasoning about it, never the opponent's move.
chess_log.narrative_3x3_moment_framing: [One connected decision follows, in order: Why1 = the player's intent, Why2 = what was wrong with their move, Why3 = why the better move is better (often the same underlying point as Why2, restated from a different angle, not always a distinct second step), Why4 = the lesson for next time. Either Why2 or Why3, or both, may be blank -- treat a blank as simply unanswered, not a gap.]
chess_log.classifier:
Classify each of these player self-notes about a chess move as SHALLOW or DEEP.

The question is simple: does the note give the player something to learn from about this move? A DEEP note diagnoses the mistake, even briefly. A SHALLOW note doesn't.

DEEP is the normal case. Check the SHALLOW patterns below first. If none of them fits, the note is DEEP. If you are unsure whether a pattern fits, choose DEEP.

SHALLOW: the note gives no diagnosis of this move. That means one of these patterns:

1. It only says the player doesn't understand, can't follow, or doesn't see why the move was bad or why the engine move is better, and says nothing concrete about this position. A remark about the size of the mistake (CPL, the eval drop) adds no diagnosis. Neither does a guess about the engine's general taste ("it must be positional", "the engine likes the bishop pair") that the player doesn't tie to a piece, square, threat or plan on this board.
     "I can't tell what's wrong with it."
     "Engine line is beyond me. Lost a lot of eval though."
     "No idea. Maybe the engine just likes having two bishops."

2. It isn't about the move at all: a note to ignore the game, a placeholder, an abandoned or disconnected game.
     "Placeholder, skip this one."
     "Opponent left after move 2."

3. It writes the move off as pointless, as accomplishing nothing, or as having no purpose, and adds only the result, without saying what the player missed, intended, or should have played instead. Calling a move passive, weak or bad is not writing it off.
     "Did nothing useful and let them win a pawn."

4. Its only explanation is that the player thought the move was fine or safe, or a denial of some motive, without saying what made it unsafe.
     "Didn't mean anything by it, it looked safe."

5. It dismisses the moment because the position was already lost or the player should have resigned, and gives no lesson about the move.
     "Position was hopeless by then, nothing to learn here."

6. It calls the move a repeat of an earlier mistake ("same mistake", "again", "second time") and adds only a fact about the board, not what the player missed or intended.
     "Did it again, the e5 square was covered."
   Compare: "Again I missed the back-rank mate; I didn't see their rook could reach e1." That is DEEP, because it says what the player didn't see.

DEEP: everything else. A note is DEEP when it names anything concrete about this move, even in a few words and even as a bare fact:
  - A piece, square, tactic or threat that was hung, missed or overlooked.
  - What the player intended or was focused on, even tentatively.
  - A better move or plan, with what it would have achieved.
  - A miscount or miscalculation that is spelled out.
  - "I'm not sure why" or "I don't understand", followed by a guess that names a piece, square, threat or plan in this position.
  Examples:
    "Hung the knight on c3."
    "Missed the fork on e6."
    "I was trying to open the f-file, but my bishop was left loose."
    "Not sure why it's bad. Maybe because it lets their queen reach h4."
    "Rxd4 wins a pawn and keeps the rook active."

Judge each note on its own words.

Return one line per note: <index>: SHALLOW or <index>: DEEP.
chess_log.classifier_3x3:
Classify each 3x3 self-analysis of a chess move. You give FOUR independent
verdicts per note: one for each Why answer. The answers DO NOT rescue each
other — judge every answer on its own words.

A 3x3 self-analysis answers four questions:
  Why1 — "{why1_q}"
  Why2 — "{why2_q}"
  Why3 — "{why3_q}"
  Why4 — "{why4_q}"

Judge Why1, Why2, Why3 as INTENT (one of SPECIFIC, GENERIC, BLANK).
Judge Why4 as LESSON (one of REAL, FILLER, BLANK).

Do NOT let one answer change the verdict for another. A specific Why1 does
not make a filler Lesson real. A real Lesson does not make a generic Why1
specific. Each answer is scored on its own text.

INTENT (for Why1, Why2, Why3)
=============================
Read each answer together with the other answers for the same move. An answer may lean on another one ("It wasn't under attack" after "I was guarding my knight"). Judge what it says in that context. Still give each answer its own verdict.

BLANK: an empty answer. A blank answer is never GENERIC.

GENERIC is rare. Use it only for a non-blank answer that says nothing about this game: no piece, square, plan, threat, outcome or reason, even when read with the other answers. Such an answer could be pasted under any move of any game.
  Examples:
    "Just a good-looking move."
    "Seemed like the thing to do."
    "No real reason."
    "Just a normal move."

  Text that is not meaningful language (placeholder text, gibberish, random
  letters, keyboard mashing) counts as nothing. Judge the answer only on its
  meaningful words; if those are generic, the answer is GENERIC however long it is.
    "Wanted to keep developing. asdkj qwe zzzz xcvb mnop qwe zzzz xcvb."

SPECIFIC is everything else. All of these are SPECIFIC:
  - A piece, square, plan, tactic or threat:
      "Clearing the e-file for my rook."
      "It left my f2 pawn without a defender."
  - An outcome, even a big one:
      "I'd have won the exchange."
      "That line wins the game."
  - An answer that leans on another answer, or contradicts it:
      "That plan was already done."
      "It wasn't a safe trade after all."
  - An honest admission of not understanding, or "I'm not sure" followed by a thought. Never treat an honest answer as GENERIC.
      "I still can't see why the engine prefers it."
      "Not sure, but trading into the endgame looked good."

LESSON (for Why4)
=================
When in doubt, choose REAL.

REAL: the lesson points at something to do or change next game. That can be a habit, a check, a method, an area of chess to pay more attention to, or a chess quality to play with more or less of (activity, aggression, patience). It counts if it is short. It counts if it is phrased as a description of what went wrong, as long as that points at what to change.
  Examples:
    "Count attackers and defenders on every capture square."
    "Before every move, ask what my opponent's last move threatens."
    "Sit on my hands for ten seconds and recheck the board."
    "Push for the initiative when I'm ahead in development."
    "I was too slow to bring my rooks into the game."
    "Pay more attention to pawn structure."

FILLER: the lesson gives nothing to act on. It is a shrug, a complaint about the game, giving up, doubting yourself instead of naming a change, or a general effort word with nothing chess-specific (focus, concentrate, try harder). A lesson that names an idea and then gives up on it ("…but I can't do that") is FILLER.
  Examples:
    "Try harder."
    "Who knows."
    "Bad day at the board."
    "Concentrate more."
    "I should see more, but I'm just not good enough yet."

BLANK (for Why4): an empty lesson.

Output format
=============
Return the verdict list FIRST, before any explanation. Preferably return
ONLY the verdict list.
One line per note, exactly this shape (keep ordering WHY1 → WHY2 → WHY3 → LESSON):

<index>: WHY1=<SPECIFIC|GENERIC|BLANK> WHY2=<SPECIFIC|GENERIC|BLANK> WHY3=<SPECIFIC|GENERIC|BLANK> LESSON=<REAL|FILLER|BLANK>

Notes to classify follow, one block per index.

ai_chat.formatting_rules:
CRITICAL FORMATTING RULES - YOU MUST FOLLOW THESE:
1. NEVER use numbered lists (1., 2., 3., etc.) - write in paragraph form only
2. NEVER use bullet points (-, *, •, etc.) - write in paragraph form only
3. NEVER use headings or section breaks - write in continuous paragraph form only
4. Keep all responses SHORT - aim for 2-3 sentences maximum
5. Write in plain, continuous paragraph form with no formatting, lists, or structure
6. Be direct and to the point - no lengthy explanations unless explicitly requested
7. Moves that were NOT actually played in the game but you still want to reference must be bolded using double asterisks: **14.Re4**
8. Moves that WERE actually played in the game must be wrapped exactly as [%14.Re4] for White or [%14...Re4] for Black using the notations provided. Never bold these real moves—only use the [%move] syntax.
9. Only use the [%move] syntax for moves that exactly match the provided list of actual game moves.
